We investigate whether non-standard neutrino interactions (NSI) could be tested by observing neutrinos emitted from a future supernova (SN) in our galaxy. Working in a three-neutrino scenario, we examine how NSI would influence neutrino propagation through the supernova envelope, with particular emphasis on NSI-driven resonant flavor conversions that may occur in the highly deleptonized inner regions.

We assess the prospects for observing these NSI signatures in a megaton-scale water Cherenkov detector. Possible signals include distortions of the $\bar\nu_e$ spectrum caused by: (i) shock waves moving through the supernova envelope, (ii) temporal variations in the electron fraction, and (iii) matter effects inside the Earth. We also consider whether the neutronization burst of $\nu_e$ could be detected.

Our results indicate that the $\bar\nu_e$ spectrum may show striking features produced by internal resonant conversions induced by NSI. Such effects arise when non-universal NSI couplings are at the level of a few percent, and when flavor-changing NSI are extremely small but exceed a few $\times 10^{-5}$.

The study investigates whether non-standard neutrino interactions (NSI) could be tested using the neutrino signal from a future galactic supernova. Because a core-collapse supernova produces an intense burst of neutrinos of all flavors, it offers a unique environment in which even small deviations from standard neutrino physics may leave observable imprints.

The analysis considers the effects of NSI on neutrino propagation through the supernova envelope in a three-neutrino framework. In addition to the usual matter effects described by the Mikheyev–Smirnov–Wolfenstein mechanism, the study includes possible new interactions between neutrinos and matter. These interactions can modify the effective matter potential experienced by neutrinos as they travel outward from the dense supernova core, thereby altering flavor conversion probabilities.

A particular focus is placed on NSI-induced resonant flavor conversions that may occur in the highly deleptonised inner layers of the supernova. In these regions, the electron fraction is very low, which can create conditions for new resonances that are absent in the standard scenario. Such resonances can lead to significant conversions between neutrino flavors, especially between electron-type neutrinos or antineutrinos and the other flavors.

The study discusses several possible observational signatures that could help identify or constrain NSI effects in a future supernova neutrino signal. These include spectral modulations caused by shock-wave propagation through the stellar envelope, time-dependent changes associated with the evolution of the electron fraction, Earth matter effects if the neutrinos pass through the Earth before detection, and the observation of the prompt neutronization burst of electron neutrinos. Each of these signatures could provide complementary information about how neutrinos have transformed during propagation.

The results suggest that the electron antineutrino spectrum, in particular, may exhibit dramatic features caused by NSI. Such effects could arise if non-universal NSI strengths are at the level of a few percent, or if flavor-changing NSI are present at very small values, above a few × 10⁻⁵. Therefore, a high-statistics observation of neutrinos from a future galactic supernova could provide a sensitive probe of non-standard neutrino interactions, potentially reaching parameter regions that are difficult to test in terrestrial experiments.

The study investigates the possibility of using neutrinos from a future galactic supernova as a probe of non-standard neutrino interactions (NSI). In addition to the standard weak interactions responsible for neutrino production, propagation, and detection, many extensions of the Standard Model allow neutrinos to have small additional interactions with matter. Although such effects may be extremely weak, the dense environment of a core-collapse supernova can greatly amplify their impact on neutrino flavor evolution.

The analysis considers three-flavor neutrino propagation through the supernova envelope, including both the ordinary matter-induced Mikheyev–Smirnov–Wolfenstein effect and additional matter potentials generated by NSI. These non-standard interactions may be flavor non-universal, meaning that different neutrino flavors experience different effective matter potentials, or flavor-changing, meaning that the interaction can directly mix different flavors while the neutrinos travel through matter. In the high-density regions inside the supernova, even very small NSI parameters can create new resonant flavor-conversion channels that do not occur in the standard oscillation scenario.

Particular attention is given to NSI-induced resonant conversions occurring deep inside the supernova, before the neutrinos encounter the usual outer MSW resonance regions. Such internal resonances can strongly modify the flavor composition of the emitted neutrino fluxes. Since the original spectra of electron antineutrinos, electron neutrinos, and non-electron flavors are expected to differ, these flavor conversions can leave observable imprints on the neutrino signal detected at Earth.

The study then evaluates how these effects would appear in a large water Cherenkov detector with a fiducial mass of order one Megaton. Such a detector would observe a galactic supernova primarily through inverse beta decay, \(\bar\nu_e + p \rightarrow e^+ + n\), making it especially sensitive to changes in the electron antineutrino spectrum. The predicted event spectra are calculated for different choices of NSI parameters and compared with the expectations from standard neutrino oscillations.

The results show that non-standard interactions can produce striking distortions in the detected \(\bar\nu_e\) energy spectrum. In particular, flavor non-universal NSI with strengths of only a few percent relative to the standard weak interaction can lead to dramatic spectral features. Even more remarkably, flavor-changing NSI can be probed down to values above a few \(\times 10^{-5}\), far smaller than many existing experimental limits. These small interactions become observable because the enormous matter density and long propagation distance inside the supernova provide an exceptionally sensitive environment for matter-enhanced flavor transformation.

The study concludes that neutrinos from a future galactic core-collapse supernova would offer a powerful test of non-standard neutrino interactions. A high-statistics observation in a Megaton-scale water Cherenkov detector could reveal or constrain NSI effects through characteristic changes in the supernova \(\bar\nu_e\) signal. Therefore, supernova neutrinos represent a uniquely sensitive probe of physics beyond the Standard Model, capable of testing extremely small deviations from standard neutrino matter interactions.

A next-generation **Megaton Cherenkov** detector would be a powerful tool for studying neutrino physics beyond the Standard Model, including possible **NSI** — non-standard interactions of neutrinos with matter. In such a detector, enormous volumes of ultra-pure water or ice are monitored by sensitive photodetectors. When a charged particle produced by a neutrino interaction travels faster than light can move through that medium, it emits a faint cone of **Cherenkov** radiation. By reconstructing this light, scientists can infer the energy, direction, and type of the incoming neutrino.

The **Megaton** scale is especially important because neutrinos interact extremely rarely. A detector with a mass of around one million tons would collect far more events than smaller experiments, improving sensitivity to subtle effects such as NSI. These interactions could slightly modify how neutrinos oscillate as they pass through Earth, producing deviations from the predictions of standard neutrino oscillation models.

By comparing atmospheric, solar, and accelerator neutrino data, a Megaton Cherenkov experiment could place strong limits on NSI parameters or perhaps reveal evidence of new physics. Such a discovery would have major implications for particle physics and cosmology, helping us understand whether neutrinos interact through unknown forces and whether the Standard Model is only part of a deeper theory.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an abstract for a physics paper on probing non-standard neutrino interactions using neutrinos from a future galactic supernova, including effects in the supernova envelope and possible detector signatures.
counterfactuals.output:
We investigate the sensitivity of a future Galactic core-collapse supernova neutrino burst to non-standard neutrino interactions (NSI) in matter. We focus on neutral-current-like NSI with electrons and nucleons, which modify the effective matter potential experienced by neutrinos as they propagate through the supernova envelope. These interactions can alter flavor evolution through shifts in the Mikheyev–Smirnov–Wolfenstein resonances, the appearance of additional NSI-induced level crossings, and modified collective or turbulence-affected conversion patterns, depending on the strength and flavor structure of the new couplings. We study the resulting impact on the time-, energy-, and flavor-dependent neutrino signal expected at terrestrial detectors.

Using representative supernova density profiles and neutrino emission models, we compute flavor survival probabilities in the presence of standard oscillations and NSI, including the dependence on the neutrino mass ordering and on the location of resonant transitions in the stellar envelope. We then assess observable consequences in large water Cherenkov, liquid scintillator, and liquid-argon detectors through inverse beta decay, elastic scattering, and charged-current interactions on argon. We identify characteristic detector signatures of NSI, including distortions of the prompt neutronization burst, energy-dependent swaps in the electron-flavor spectra, changes in the relative event rates among detector channels, and time-dependent modulations associated with shock-wave propagation through the resonance region.

Our results show that a high-statistics observation of a Galactic supernova can probe regions of NSI parameter space complementary to terrestrial oscillation experiments and coherent elastic neutrino-nucleus scattering measurements. In particular, correlations between the electron-neutrino signal in liquid argon and the antineutrino signal in water or scintillator detectors provide a robust handle on flavor-changing and non-universal NSI in the supernova envelope. We conclude that the next Galactic supernova will offer a unique laboratory for testing matter-induced new physics in the neutrino sector, provided that multi-detector data and realistic supernova modeling are combined in a global analysis.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize a study of NSI effects on three-flavor supernova neutrino propagation and how they could be detected in a Megaton water Cherenkov detector.
counterfactuals.output:
A study of non-standard neutrino interactions (NSI) in three-flavor supernova neutrino propagation typically examines how additional matter-induced flavor-changing or non-universal interactions modify the Mikheyev–Smirnov–Wolfenstein flavor evolution of neutrinos emerging from a core-collapse supernova, and whether those modifications could be seen in a large water Cherenkov detector.

## Main idea

In the Standard Model, supernova neutrinos undergo flavor conversion because they propagate through dense matter. The effective matter potential depends mainly on the electron density and produces the familiar solar-scale and atmospheric-scale MSW resonances.

With NSI, the matter Hamiltonian is modified by extra terms of the form

\[
H_{\rm mat} \sim \sqrt{2}G_F N_e
\begin{pmatrix}
1+\epsilon_{ee} & \epsilon_{e\mu} & \epsilon_{e\tau}\\
\epsilon_{e\mu}^* & \epsilon_{\mu\mu} & \epsilon_{\mu\tau}\\
\epsilon_{e\tau}^* & \epsilon_{\mu\tau}^* & \epsilon_{\tau\tau}
\end{pmatrix},
\]

where the \(\epsilon_{\alpha\beta}\) parameters describe non-standard interactions with matter. Even values allowed by laboratory and oscillation bounds can noticeably alter flavor conversion inside a supernova.

## Propagation effects studied

The study follows three-flavor neutrino evolution through a realistic supernova density profile, including:

1. **Standard MSW resonances**
   - The high-density atmospheric resonance, associated with \(\Delta m^2_{31}\) and \(\theta_{13}\).
   - The low-density solar resonance, associated with \(\Delta m^2_{21}\) and \(\theta_{12}\).

2. **NSI-induced resonances**
   - NSI can create an additional internal resonance, often called an **I-resonance**, in regions where the electron fraction \(Y_e\) takes values near those relevant for supernova ejecta.
   - This resonance can occur deep inside the star, before the usual MSW resonances.
   - It can swap or partially swap \(\nu_e\), \(\bar\nu_e\), and non-electron flavors.

3. **Dependence on mass hierarchy and mixing**
   - The impact depends on whether the neutrino mass ordering is normal or inverted.
   - It also depends on \(\theta_{13}\), the shock-wave profile, and the magnitude/sign of NSI parameters such as \(\epsilon_{\tau\tau}\), \(\epsilon_{e\tau}\), or combinations involving down-quark couplings.

4. **Energy-dependent spectral distortions**
   - NSI can change the survival probabilities \(P(\nu_e\to\nu_e)\) and \(P(\bar\nu_e\to\bar\nu_e)\).
   - Since supernova \(\nu_e\), \(\bar\nu_e\), and \(\nu_x\) spectra generally have different average energies and luminosities, altered flavor conversion produces detectable changes in the observed energy spectra.

## Observable signal in a Megaton water Cherenkov detector

A Megaton-scale water Cherenkov detector would be dominated by inverse beta decay:

\[
\bar\nu_e + p \rightarrow e^+ + n.
\]

This channel gives a large sample of positron events, potentially hundreds of thousands for a Galactic supernova at \(\sim 10\) kpc.

Other channels are subdominant but useful:

- Elastic scattering on electrons:
  \[
  \nu + e^- \rightarrow \nu + e^-,
  \]
  which is forward-peaked and helps locate the supernova.
- Charged-current interactions on oxygen:
  \[
  \nu_e + {}^{16}{\rm O}, \quad \bar\nu_e + {}^{16}{\rm O},
  \]
  which are sensitive to higher-energy neutrinos.
- Neutral-current oxygen excitation, which probes the total flux of all flavors.

## Detection strategy

The study argues that NSI could be detected through deviations from the expected standard-oscillation signal, such as:

1. **Modified positron energy spectrum**
   - If NSI cause a stronger admixture of hotter \(\nu_x\) flux into the \(\bar\nu_e\) channel, the inverse-beta spectrum becomes harder.
   - If they suppress this admixture, the spectrum becomes softer.

2. **Changes in event rates**
   - The total number of inverse-beta events can change because the \(\bar\nu_e\) flux and average energy are altered.

3. **Time-dependent distortions**
   - As the supernova shock wave moves through MSW resonance regions, the survival probabilities can change with time.
   - NSI can shift or add features to these time variations.

4. **Comparison of detection channels**
   - Inverse beta decay mainly probes \(\bar\nu_e\).
   - Elastic scattering and oxygen events provide additional information about \(\nu_e\) and high-energy components.
   - A mismatch among these channels relative to standard expectations could indicate NSI.

5. **Hierarchy discrimination**
   - Some NSI signatures mimic a change in mass ordering, while others produce effects not reproducible by standard oscillations.
   - A large detector with high statistics could help separate NSI effects from normal/inverted hierarchy scenarios.

## Main conclusion

The central conclusion is that NSI can substantially modify three-flavor supernova neutrino flavor conversion, even for coupling strengths allowed by existing limits. These effects may appear as additional resonances, altered survival probabilities, spectral swaps, or changes in the time and energy structure of the detected \(\bar\nu_e\) signal.

A Megaton water Cherenkov detector would have enough statistics from a Galactic supernova to observe such distortions, especially in the inverse-beta-decay positron spectrum. However, identifying NSI unambiguously would require controlling astrophysical uncertainties in the original supernova fluxes and combining information from multiple detection channels and possibly multiple detectors.

We summarize how NSI in matter alter the Mikheyev–Smirnov–Wolfenstein resonance structure, potentially shifting or creating flavor transitions during propagation through the stellar envelope. These effects can interplay with shock-wave passage, producing time-dependent spectral modulations, and may influence the neutrino-driven electron fraction evolution relevant for nucleosynthesis. The prompt neutronization burst, dominated by electron neutrinos, provides a particularly clean diagnostic of matter-induced flavor transformation and may help distinguish NSI from standard oscillation scenarios. Additional regeneration effects from terrestrial matter can further modify the detected signal, offering complementary sensitivity to NSI parameters. counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a research-paper abstract describing how NSI-induced resonant conversions in the inner layers of a supernova could modify the detected antineutrino spectrum.
counterfactuals.output:
We investigate the impact of non-standard neutrino interactions (NSI) on flavor conversion in the dense inner layers of core-collapse supernovae and its imprint on the observable antineutrino signal. In the presence of flavor-dependent NSI with matter, the effective propagation Hamiltonian can develop additional resonant structures at densities well above those associated with the standard Mikheyev–Smirnov–Wolfenstein resonances. We show that such NSI-induced resonances may occur close to the neutrinosphere, where the original flavor spectra are still strongly hierarchical and where small changes in flavor evolution can lead to sizable modifications of the emerging electron-antineutrino flux. Depending on the strength and flavor structure of the NSI parameters, these resonances can trigger partial or nearly complete conversions between electron and non-electron antineutrino states, altering both the normalization and spectral shape of the antineutrino signal expected at terrestrial detectors.

We characterize the resulting modifications in terms of shifts in the average detected energy, changes in the high-energy tail, and time-dependent distortions associated with the evolving supernova density profile. In particular, if the original non-electron antineutrino spectrum is hotter than the electron-antineutrino spectrum, NSI-enhanced conversion can produce a harder detected \(\bar{\nu}_e\) spectrum and increase the event rate in water Cherenkov, liquid scintillator, and liquid argon detectors sensitive to antineutrino channels. Conversely, resonant transitions in other regions of NSI parameter space can suppress the high-energy component or generate nontrivial spectral splits. These effects may be partially degenerate with uncertainties in the primary supernova fluxes and with collective neutrino oscillations, but their occurrence at high matter density provides a distinct phenomenological handle.

Our results demonstrate that a future Galactic supernova neutrino burst could probe NSI couplings in regimes complementary to terrestrial oscillation and scattering experiments. The detection of anomalous spectral hardening, time-dependent flavor features, or deviations from standard matter-effect predictions in the antineutrino channel would provide evidence for new neutrino-matter interactions operating in extreme astrophysical environments.

counterfactuals.prompt: In formal academic style, describe the possibility of detecting non-standard neutrino interactions from a future galactic supernova, including relevant NSI parameter sensitivities and observable spectral features.
counterfactuals.output:
A future Galactic core-collapse supernova would provide an exceptionally sensitive, time-dependent neutrino source with which to probe non-standard neutrino interactions (NSI). Such interactions are commonly parameterized by effective four-fermion operators of the form

\[
\mathcal{L}_{\rm NSI}
=
-2\sqrt{2}G_F \,\epsilon_{\alpha\beta}^{fP}
(\bar{\nu}_\alpha\gamma^\mu P_L\nu_\beta)
(\bar f\gamma_\mu P f),
\]

where \(f=e,u,d\), \(P=L,R\), and \(\epsilon_{\alpha\beta}^{fP}\) quantify the strength of the new interaction relative to the Fermi constant. In supernova flavor evolution, the most relevant combinations are the matter NSI parameters

\[
\epsilon_{\alpha\beta}
=
\sum_{f=e,u,d}
\frac{n_f}{n_e}
\left(\epsilon_{\alpha\beta}^{fL}+\epsilon_{\alpha\beta}^{fR}\right),
\]

which modify the neutrino propagation Hamiltonian in matter. The diagonal parameters alter the effective matter potential, while off-diagonal parameters induce flavor-changing neutral-current effects.

In a supernova environment, even relatively small NSI can have observable consequences because neutrinos propagate through extremely large matter densities and steep density gradients. The effective matter Hamiltonian may be written schematically as

\[
H_{\rm mat}
=
\sqrt{2}G_F n_e
\begin{pmatrix}
1+\epsilon_{ee} & \epsilon_{e\mu} & \epsilon_{e\tau} \\
\epsilon_{e\mu}^{*} & \epsilon_{\mu\mu} & \epsilon_{\mu\tau} \\
\epsilon_{e\tau}^{*} & \epsilon_{\mu\tau}^{*} & \epsilon_{\tau\tau}
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

Thus, a Galactic supernova neutrino burst would be sensitive not only to the standard Mikheyev–Smirnov–Wolfenstein resonances but also to additional resonances or modified adiabaticity conditions induced by NSI.

A particularly important signature is the possible occurrence of an “internal” or “I-resonance,” associated with the condition that the effective \(e\)-flavor matter potential changes sign or becomes degenerate with another flavor state. In simplified two-flavor language, this can occur when

\[
Y_e + \epsilon_{\rm eff} \simeq 0,
\]

where \(Y_e\) is the electron fraction and \(\epsilon_{\rm eff}\) is an appropriate combination of diagonal NSI parameters, often involving differences such as \(\epsilon_{ee}-\epsilon_{\tau\tau}\) or \(\epsilon_{ee}-\epsilon_{\mu\mu}\). Since the electron fraction in the inner supernova envelope can be \(Y_e \sim 0.3\)–0.5, diagonal NSI of order

\[
|\epsilon_{ee}-\epsilon_{\tau\tau}| \sim 0.1-1
\]

can substantially modify the flavor evolution, depending on the underlying model and matter composition. Such values are within the range where supernova observations can provide information complementary to terrestrial oscillation and scattering experiments.

Observable consequences would depend on the neutrino mass ordering, the explosion model, the time after core bounce, and the still uncertain role of collective neutrino-neutrino flavor conversion. Nevertheless, several robust classes of signatures may be identified.

First, NSI could modify the neutronization burst, the prompt \(\nu_e\)-dominated emission occurring within the first \(\sim 10\)–30 ms after core bounce. This phase is especially clean theoretically because the emitted flux is dominated by electron neutrinos. In the standard scenario, the survival probability of the neutronization burst is strongly dependent on the mass ordering, especially in liquid-argon detectors such as DUNE, which are primarily sensitive to \(\nu_e\) through

\[
\nu_e + {}^{40}{\rm Ar} \rightarrow e^- + {}^{40}{\rm K}^{*}.
\]

NSI-induced flavor conversion could suppress, restore, or distort the expected neutronization peak. A statistically significant departure from the standard burst amplitude or time profile in DUNE would therefore provide a sensitive probe of flavor-changing and non-universal NSI involving \(\nu_e\).

Second, NSI may alter the energy spectra of the accretion and cooling phases. Standard oscillation physics can produce spectral swaps or splits, where the flavor content changes sharply above or below a characteristic energy. NSI can shift the split energy, wash out a swap, or generate additional step-like spectral structures. Observable features could include a hardening or softening of the detected \(\bar\nu_e\) spectrum in water Cherenkov and scintillator detectors, a modified \(\nu_e\) spectrum in argon, or inconsistent flavor temperatures inferred from different detection channels.

Third, NSI may affect the imprint of shock-wave propagation. In the standard picture, as the supernova shock passes through the MSW resonance region, the changing density profile can produce time-dependent modulations in the detected neutrino signal. NSI can move the resonance radii, introduce additional resonances, or change the degree of adiabaticity. The resulting signal may contain anomalous time-dependent spectral distortions, such as dips or shoulders in the event-rate evolution at fixed energy.

Fourth, flavor-changing NSI, particularly parameters such as \(\epsilon_{e\tau}\), \(\epsilon_{e\mu}\), or \(\epsilon_{\mu\tau}\), can generate new off-diagonal matter mixing. Present terrestrial bounds are generally strongest on \(\epsilon_{e\mu}\), while \(\epsilon_{e\tau}\) and certain diagonal differences are less tightly constrained. A high-statistics Galactic supernova could therefore be especially valuable for testing parameter regions such as

\[
|\epsilon_{e\tau}| \sim 10^{-3}-10^{-1},
\qquad
|\epsilon_{\mu\tau}| \sim 10^{-2}-10^{-1},
\]

depending on the supernova distance, detector capabilities, assumed priors on the primary spectra, and degeneracies with standard oscillation parameters. Sensitivity to diagonal differences such as

\[
|\epsilon_{ee}-\epsilon_{\tau\tau}|,\,
|\epsilon_{ee}-\epsilon_{\mu\mu}|
\sim 10^{-2}-10^{-1}
\]

may be achievable in favorable scenarios, especially if clear spectral or temporal features are observed. However, robust quantitative bounds are model-dependent, and values at the level of a few percent should be interpreted as optimistic, scenario-specific sensitivities rather than universal guarantees.

The observational prospects would be strongest for a supernova at a distance of order 10 kpc, for which next-generation and currently operating detectors would record very large event samples. Hyper-Kamiokande would measure tens of thousands to hundreds of thousands of inverse beta decay events,

\[
\bar\nu_e+p\rightarrow e^+ + n,
\]

providing excellent statistics for the \(\bar\nu_e\) light curve and energy spectrum. JUNO would deliver high-resolution scintillator measurements of \(\bar\nu_e\) spectra and neutral-current channels. DUNE would be uniquely sensitive to the \(\nu_e\) component, especially the neutronization burst. IceCube, while lacking event-by-event energy reconstruction, would provide sub-millisecond timing precision for the overall \(\bar\nu_e\)-dominated luminosity evolution. A combined analysis would therefore allow one to compare the \(\nu_e\), \(\bar\nu_e\), and non-electron flavor sectors, which is essential for disentangling NSI from uncertainties in the supernova emission model.

The clearest evidence for NSI would not necessarily be a simple excess or deficit of events, but rather a correlated pattern of anomalies across detectors and time phases. Examples include: an unexpectedly absent or enhanced neutronization burst; energy-dependent spectral swaps incompatible with standard MSW conversion; time-dependent distortions not aligned with standard shock-wave propagation; differences between the flavor temperatures inferred from argon, water Cherenkov, and scintillator detectors; or a signal favoring a mass-ordering interpretation inconsistent with terrestrial measurements. Such features would be especially compelling if they appeared with the characteristic energy and time dependence expected from matter-induced flavor conversion.

In summary, a Galactic supernova would constitute a powerful laboratory for non-standard neutrino interactions. NSI parameters at the level of approximately \(10^{-2}\)–\(10^{-1}\) in favorable flavor channels could leave detectable imprints on the supernova neutrino signal, while order-unity diagonal NSI could qualitatively alter the flavor-conversion pattern through additional resonances. The most promising observables are the \(\nu_e\) neutronization burst, energy-dependent spectral swaps or splits, shock-induced temporal modulations, and multi-detector inconsistencies in the reconstructed flavor spectra. Although precise sensitivities will depend on the supernova model, distance, mass ordering, detector response, and collective oscillation physics, the observation of a nearby supernova would provide a uniquely complementary test of NSI beyond the reach of terrestrial experiments alone.
